youtube.title: Kodak Invented the Digital Camera in 1975 and Saw Its Own End Coming
youtube.description:
In 1975 a Kodak engineer built the first digital camera. In 1981, Kodak's own research told its leaders that digital could replace film and that they had about ten years to prepare. In 2012 Kodak filed for bankruptcy. So why did a company that saw the future, patented it and put a date on it still lose to it?

This documentary follows the prototype, the 1979 and 1981 warnings, the decade of choices that kept film first, and the chain that followed: the dividend cut, the exit from the Dow, the phone that absorbed the camera, the bankruptcy filing and the patents sold for a fraction of their estimated value. Every figure comes with its source on screen.

youtube.comment: If you'd run Kodak in 1981 with ten years' warning, would you have killed film yourself? 👇

sources.claim: Eastman Kodak filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on January 19, 2012, in New York
sources.source: Voluntary petition, In re Eastman Kodak Co., Case No. 12-10202, US Bankruptcy Court, Southern District of New York, 19 January 2012

sources.claim: Kodak listed liabilities of $6.75 billion
sources.source: Kodak Chapter 11 petition, 19 January 2012; reported by The New York Times, 19 January 2012

sources.claim: In 1975 a Kodak engineer, Steven Sasson, built the first digital camera
sources.source: Kodak; The New York Times Lens blog, 'Kodak's First Digital Moment', 12 August 2015

sources.claim: The prototype weighed eight pounds, recorded 10,000-pixel (0.01 megapixel) black-and-white images to cassette tape, and took 23 seconds per image
sources.source: The New York Times Lens blog, 12 August 2015; Steven Sasson's account published by Kodak

sources.claim: Sasson was 24 and built the camera around a Fairchild CCD sensor, a movie-camera lens and a cassette recorder
sources.source: The New York Times Lens blog, 12 August 2015

sources.claim: By Sasson's account, the first image appeared on the television screen in December 1975
sources.source: Steven Sasson, 'We Had No Idea', Kodak 'A Thousand Words' blog, 16 October 2007; The New York Times Lens blog, 12 August 2015

sources.claim: Management's reaction: 'that's cute — but don't tell anyone about it'
sources.source: Steven Sasson, quoted in The New York Times, 'At Kodak, Clinging to a Future Beyond Film', 2 May 2008

sources.claim: Managers asked why anyone would want to look at their pictures on a television
sources.source: Steven Sasson recollection, The New York Times Lens blog, 12 August 2015

sources.claim: US Patent 4,131,919, 'Electronic Still Camera', granted 26 December 1978 to Gareth A. Lloyd and Steven J. Sasson, assigned to Eastman Kodak
sources.source: US Patent and Trademark Office, patent 4,131,919, 26 December 1978

sources.claim: In 1979 a Kodak executive wrote a report on how markets would switch from film to digital, government first, then professionals, then the mass market, by 2010
sources.source: The Economist, 'The last Kodak moment?', 14 January 2012 (interview with former Kodak executive Larry Matteson)

sources.claim: Sony announced the Mavica, storing still images on a magnetic disk, on 25 August 1981; the original Mavica was never sold commercially
sources.source: Sony corporate history, 'Sony Mavica'

sources.claim: In 1981 Kodak's head of market intelligence, Vince Barabba, ran a study concluding digital could replace film and Kodak had approximately ten years to prepare
sources.source: Vince Barabba, quoted in Chunka Mui, 'How Kodak Failed', Forbes, 18 January 2012; Vince Barabba, 'The Decision Loom', 2011

sources.claim: Chunka Mui, drawing on Barabba's account, argues Kodak used digital to support film rather than prepare for its replacement
sources.source: Chunka Mui, 'How Kodak Failed', Forbes, 18 January 2012

sources.claim: Kodak's profit peaked at $2.5 billion in 1999
sources.source: The Economist, 'The last Kodak moment?', 14 January 2012

sources.claim: Kodak scientists built the first megapixel sensor, 1.4 million pixels, in 1986
sources.source: Kodak corporate history, 'Milestones'

sources.claim: In 1991 Kodak introduced the DCS, a professional digital camera system aimed at photojournalists
sources.source: Kodak corporate history, 'Milestones'

sources.claim: Kodak launched the Advanced Photo System under the Advantix brand in 1996, a format developed with Fujifilm, Canon, Minolta and Nikon
sources.source: Eastman Kodak announcement of the Advanced Photo System, February 1996; The New York Times, February 1996

sources.claim: Kodak's Advantix Preview camera let users preview shots on a screen, but still recorded them on film; Kodak spent more than $500 million developing and launching it
sources.source: Chunka Mui, 'How Kodak Failed', Forbes, 18 January 2012

sources.claim: George Eastman sold the first Kodak camera in 1888 with the slogan 'You press the button, we do the rest'
sources.source: Kodak corporate history; Kodak advertising, 1888

sources.claim: In 1976 Kodak accounted for 90% of film and 85% of camera sales in the United States
sources.source: Harvard Business School case 'Kodak and the Digital Revolution (A)', Giovanni Gavetti et al., 2005

sources.claim: Kodak joined the Dow Jones Industrial Average in 1930
sources.source: S&P Dow Jones Indices, DJIA component history; Dow Jones Indexes announcement, 1 April 2004

sources.claim: Kodak employed 145,300 people worldwide in 1988
sources.source: Eastman Kodak Annual Report 1988

sources.claim: Kodak's revenue peaked at nearly $16 billion in 1996
sources.source: Eastman Kodak Annual Report 1996; The Economist, 14 January 2012

sources.claim: Kodak introduced its first consumer digital camera, the DC40, in 1995
sources.source: Kodak corporate history, 'Milestones'

sources.claim: Kodak said in September 2003 that demand for traditional film was declining as digital grew, and cut its dividend by 72% to fund a shift to digital
sources.source: Eastman Kodak press release and investor presentation, 25 September 2003

sources.claim: Kodak was removed from the Dow Jones Industrial Average on 8 April 2004 after 74 years
sources.source: Dow Jones Indexes announcement, 1 April 2004

sources.claim: Kodak led US digital camera sales in 2005
sources.source: IDC, reported by The New York Times, 2 May 2008

sources.claim: Apple unveiled the iPhone, with a built-in camera, on 9 January 2007
sources.source: Apple press release, 9 January 2007

sources.claim: On 10 January 2007 Kodak announced it would sell its Health Group to Onex for up to $2.55 billion
sources.source: Eastman Kodak press release, 10 January 2007

sources.claim: Kodachrome represented a fraction of 1 percent of Kodak's still-film sales; Kodak retired it on 22 June 2009 after 74 years
sources.source: Eastman Kodak press release, 22 June 2009

sources.claim: Samsung agreed to pay Kodak about $550 million in a patent settlement
sources.source: Eastman Kodak announcement, December 2009; reported by Reuters, December 2009
Eastman Kodak annual reports and Form 10-K filings, 1996-2011

sources.claim: Kodak posted a net loss in each year from 2008 to 2011
sources.source: Eastman Kodak Form 10-K filings, 2008-2011

sources.claim: On 30 September 2011 Kodak shares fell more than 50% after it hired restructuring lawyers
sources.source: The Wall Street Journal and Reuters, 30 September 2011

sources.claim: Citigroup provided $950 million of debtor-in-possession financing
sources.source: Eastman Kodak press release, 19 January 2012

sources.claim: Kodak sold Kodak Gallery to Shutterfly for $23.8 million
sources.source: Shutterfly press release, March 2012

sources.claim: Facebook agreed to buy Instagram, then with 13 employees, for $1 billion on 9 April 2012
sources.source: Facebook announcement, 9 April 2012; The New York Times, 9 April 2012

sources.claim: An earlier analysis valued Kodak's imaging patents at $2.2 billion to $2.6 billion
sources.source: MDB Capital Group analysis, 2011; reported by Bloomberg, December 2012

sources.claim: Kodak sold about 1,100 digital imaging patents for about $525 million to a group including Apple, Google and Microsoft
sources.source: Eastman Kodak press release, 19 December 2012

sources.claim: Kodak transferred its film, paper, kiosk and document imaging businesses to the UK Kodak Pension Plan for $650 million, creating Kodak Alaris
sources.source: Eastman Kodak press release, 29 April 2013

sources.claim: Kodak emerged from bankruptcy on 3 September 2013 as a company focused on commercial printing
sources.source: Eastman Kodak press release, 3 September 2013

sources.claim: Kodak had about 17,000 employees at the time of the filing
sources.source: The New York Times, 19 January 2012

sources.claim: Kodak-branded consumer cameras are made by JK Imaging under licence
sources.source: JK Imaging / Eastman Kodak licensing announcement, January 2013

sources.claim: Steven Sasson was named a recipient of the National Medal of Technology and Innovation for 2009
sources.source: White House announcement, 2009 National Medal of Technology and Innovation laureates

sources.claim: Fujifilm announced 5,000 job cuts in January 2006 and moved into medical imaging, display films and cosmetics
sources.source: Reuters, 31 January 2006; The Economist, 'The last Kodak moment?', 14 January 2012
